claims.text: Maintaining a nanoscale grain structure enhances the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Abundant grain boundaries act as sinks for diffusing species.
Grain-boundary sink behavior limits elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
A refractory high-entropy alloy can be produced by laser powder bed fusion using in-situ alloy formation from elemental powders.
The initial additively manufactured alloy exhibits a dendritic or cellular microstructure with nanoscale grains.
Lower-temperature annealing preserves nanoscale grains, whereas higher-temperature annealing produces grain coarsening.
Refractory high-entropy alloys are relevant to high-temperature aerospace and chemical-industry applications.
Temperatures above 1000 °C represent the intended exposure regime for the proposed comparison.
High configurational entropy favors a single-phase structure.
Nanoscale grain boundaries act both as barriers and as sinks for diffusing atoms.
The combined effects of configurational entropy and grain boundaries restrict diffusion-driven segregation and undesired secondary-phase formation at high temperature.
A nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy can exhibit high thermal stability and no detectable grain growth under the reported extreme-environment testing.
Samples retaining nanoscale grains will show less elemental segregation and greater retention of a single-phase microstructure than coarsened-grain samples.
Coarsened-grain samples will show more phase decomposition or secondary-phase development than nanograined samples.
Grain coarsening reduces the amount of grain-boundary area relative to a nanograined baseline.
Oxidation, irradiation, or stress-induced segregation may change the proposed grain-boundary-mediated behavior.
